title: Why Earth has seasons: it leans
dek: A tilted planet and a common wrong guess about distance, in short steps (a CI fixture).

misconception.claim: Earth has seasons because it is closer to the Sun in summer.

states.alt: The Sun is on the left and Earth is on the right. The time of year is June. Earth’s axis is tilted by 23.4 degrees and points the same way all year. The northern half leans toward the Sun and the southern half leans away from it. A pin in the north is marked warm, and a pin in the south is marked cool. In the north, Ray the sunbeam arrives from high in the sky and lands on a small patch of ground. In the south, Ray arrives at a low angle and spreads over a wide patch of ground. The picture draws the eye to the axis.

Earth circles the Sun, seen from above, on an orbit drawn to scale that looks almost like a circle. The time of year is June. Earth’s axis is tilted by 23.4 degrees and points the same way all year. The northern half leans toward the Sun and the southern half leans away from it. A pin in the north is marked warm, and a pin in the south is marked cool. The picture draws the eye to Earth.

Earth circles the Sun, seen from above, on an orbit stretched so that the nearest and farthest points show. The time of year is January. Earth’s axis is tilted by 23.4 degrees and points the same way all year. The southern half leans toward the Sun and the northern half leans away from it. A pin in the north is marked cool, and a pin in the south is marked warm. The picture draws the eye to the orbit.

The northern half leans toward the Sun and the southern half leans away from it. A pin in the north is marked warm, and a pin in the south is marked cool. The picture draws the eye to Ray.

The Sun is on the left and Earth is on the right. The time of year is December. Earth’s axis is tilted by 23.4 degrees and points the same way all year. The southern half leans toward the Sun and the northern half leans away from it. A pin in the north is marked cool, and a pin in the south is marked warm. In the north, Ray the sunbeam arrives at a low angle and spreads over a wide patch of ground. In the south, Ray arrives from high in the sky and lands on a small patch of ground. The picture draws the eye to the pin in the south.

Earth circles the Sun, seen from above, on an orbit drawn to scale that looks almost like a circle. The time of year is March. Earth’s axis is tilted by 23.4 degrees and points the same way all year. Neither half leans toward the Sun or away from it. A pin in the north is marked neither warm nor cool, and a pin in the south is marked neither warm nor cool. The picture draws the eye to the axis.

Earth circles the Sun, seen from above, on an orbit drawn to scale that looks almost like a circle. The time of year is June. Earth’s axis is tilted by 23.4 degrees and points the same way all year. The northern half leans toward the Sun and the southern half leans away from it. A pin in the north is marked warm, and a pin in the south is marked cool.

blocks.text: Earth’s axis is tilted by 23.4 degrees. Here is the trick: it keeps pointing the same way all year, toward the North Star, however far round the Sun Earth has travelled.

stops.simple: Earth is tilted, and the tilt never changes direction.

blocks.text: Picture Earth at four moments of the year. In every one of them the axis leans the same way in space. What changes is where the Sun is, compared with that lean, and that is the whole story of the year.

stops.simple: The tilt stays put while Earth moves around the Sun.

stops.prompt: Why is June so hot in Delhi?
options: Earth is closer to the Sun in June
Delhi’s half of Earth leans toward the Sun in June
The Sun burns hotter in June
stops.explain: In June the northern half of Earth leans toward the Sun, so sunlight lands steeply there and the days run long.
stops.twist: Distance is the common guess, and it is wrong: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, in the middle of northern winter.
stops.simple: June is hot in Delhi because its half of Earth leans toward the Sun.

blocks.text: Earth’s orbit is almost a circle. Its nearest and farthest distances differ by only a few percent, far too little to make a winter. Here the orbit is stretched so you can see it.

stops.simple: Earth is nearest the Sun in January, yet that is northern winter.

blocks.text: Sunlight that lands steeply is packed onto a small patch of ground. Sunlight that lands at a low angle is spread over a wide patch. Same Sun, same distance, different dose.

stops.simple: Steep light is concentrated, low light is spread out.

blocks.text: The leaning half gets something else too: long days. The Sun climbs high, stays up for many hours, and has more time to warm the ground. Steep light and long days arrive together, and together they make summer.

stops.simple: The leaning half gets steep light and long days.

stops.prompt: In December, which half of Earth leans toward the Sun?
stops.explain: Half an orbit later the same lean points away from the Sun in the north and toward it in the south.
stops.twist: Plot twist: the north did not stop leaning. The Sun moved to the other side of the lean.
stops.simple: In December the southern half leans toward the Sun.

blocks.text: Half an orbit later the picture flips. The southern half leans toward the Sun, with high light and long days. The northern half is the one with low light and short days.

stops.simple: In December the south is warm and the north is cool.

blocks.text: Twice a year Earth sits where neither half leans toward the Sun. Those are the equinoxes, in March and September. Day and night are nearly equal everywhere.

stops.simple: At the equinoxes neither half leans toward the Sun.

blocks.text: The two moments when a half leans as far as it ever does are the solstices, in June and December. Winter and summer are not the coldest and warmest days, they are the ends of the lean.

stops.simple: The solstices are when a half leans furthest.

blocks.text: The seasons are not about distance. They are about which half of Earth leans toward the Sun, and for how long the light is steep.

stops.simple: The seasons come from the lean, not from distance.

stops.prompt: It is June. Is it warm or cool in Sydney, in the southern half?
options: Cool, the southern half leans away
Warm, the southern half leans toward the Sun
stops.explain: In June the southern half leans away from the Sun, so the light is low and the days are short there.
stops.twist: The north and the south take turns, so Sydney is in winter while Delhi is in summer.

asides.title: So why do the tropics barely notice?
asides.text: Near the equator the noon Sun stays high in every season, so the tropics change far less across the year than the poles do.

asides.title: Where this stops
asides.text: Light sets the season, but weather decides how it feels. Oceans, winds, altitude and monsoons shift the hottest weeks away from the solstice.

captions: Steeper light and longer days make summer.
